distillation_scope.leaf_granularity: First-layer clinical disease leaf for the full acute appendicitis spectrum. Uncomplicated, complicated, perforated, appendiceal abscess, appendicolith-associated, pediatric, pregnancy, elderly, retrocecal, pelvic, subhepatic, left-sided, and duplicated-appendix presentations remain risk, context, anatomic, source-control, event, or future subtype axes rather than disease-name qualifiers.
distillation_scope.ranking_note: Presentation ranking may consume symptoms, vitals, inflammatory labs, exam findings, and initial imaging. Surgical pathology, intraoperative confirmation, final diagnosis, culture species or susceptibility, treatment response, and follow-up outcomes remain confirmatory or non-ranking unless a separate post-workup mode explicitly consumes them.

latent_mechanisms.clinical_meaning: Fecalith or appendicolith, lymphoid hyperplasia, edema, tumor, parasite, foreign material, stricture, or functional stasis blocks appendiceal outflow and initiates intraluminal pressure rise.

latent_mechanisms.display_name: Intraluminal pressure, venous congestion, and ischemia
latent_mechanisms.clinical_meaning: Obstructed secretions and bacterial gas raise intraluminal pressure, impair lymphatic and venous drainage, reduce mural perfusion, and predispose to gangrene or perforation.

latent_mechanisms.display_name: Enteric bacterial overgrowth and mucosal invasion
latent_mechanisms.clinical_meaning: Appendiceal stasis and ischemic mucosal injury permit polymicrobial enteric overgrowth, bacterial invasion, suppuration, and local contamination if the wall fails.
Neutrophilic inflammation, edema, mural thickening, luminal dilation, serosal irritation, and periappendiceal fat inflammation create the core local appendicitis manifold.
Early visceral midabdominal pain may migrate to focal right-lower-quadrant somatic pain when the inflamed appendix irritates parietal peritoneum; anatomic variants can blunt or relocate this pattern.

Local appendiceal infection and tissue injury drive fever, tachycardia, leukocytosis, neutrophilia, and CRP rise; these responses may be muted in frail, elderly, immunosuppressed, cirrhotic, or renal-failure contexts.

Ongoing pressure, ischemia, bacterial invasion, and transmural inflammation can progress to gangrene, microperforation, free perforation, inflammatory phlegmon, periappendiceal fluid, or drainable abscess.

latent_mechanisms.display_name: Diffuse peritonitis, sepsis, and organ-risk cascade
latent_mechanisms.clinical_meaning: Uncontrolled perforation, diffuse contamination, abscess progression, delayed source control, or host vulnerability can produce generalized peritonitis, sepsis physiology, shock, organ dysfunction, and death risk.
Appendectomy, drainage, active antibiotics, physiologic reserve, and absence of uncontrolled perforation lower bacterial burden, local inflammation, event hazards, and mortality hazard.

mechanism_edges.clinical_rationale: Appendicolith is a common obstructing context and increases complicated disease risk.
Obstruction traps mucus and gas, raising pressure and impairing drainage.
Congestion and ischemic mucosal injury permit bacterial overgrowth and invasion.
Enteric bacterial invasion elicits neutrophilic appendiceal inflammation.
Serosal and parietal peritoneal irritation localizes pain and produces focal signs.
Local infection and tissue injury trigger systemic inflammatory responses.
Mural ischemia and gangrene increase perforation risk.
Transmural inflammation can progress to gangrene, phlegmon, abscess, or perforation if uncontrolled.
Perforation or uncontrolled abscess can seed diffuse peritonitis and sepsis physiology.
Active antibiotics and procedural source control reduce viable enteric bacterial burden.
Removal or drainage of the infected focus and active therapy allow local inflammation to resolve.
Source control lowers ongoing perforation, abscess, and phlegmon progression.
Adequate control of contamination and infection reduces sepsis and organ-risk cascades.
A visible appendicolith is one measurable obstructive context, though obstruction may exist without it.
Inflamed and obstructed appendix commonly dilates on ultrasound or CT.
Appendiceal diameter above the normal range supports acute appendiceal inflammation.
Mural edema and inflammation thicken the appendiceal wall.
Serosal inflammation extends into adjacent fat, producing periappendiceal fat stranding.
Local inflammation and early contamination can produce periappendiceal or pelvic free fluid.
Severe appendiceal inflammation may secondarily thicken or inflame the cecum or terminal ileum.
Acute appendicitis usually presents with abdominal pain.
Classic pain may migrate from periumbilical or central abdomen to the right lower quadrant.
Parietal peritoneal irritation near the appendix often causes focal right-lower-quadrant pain.
Localized inflammation creates abdominal tenderness.
Focal tenderness near McBurney point supports parietal irritation in typical right-sided anatomy.
Peritoneal irritation may produce a Rovsing sign.
Guarding, rebound, or pain with movement indicate peritoneal irritation.
Visceral inflammation often produces nausea with or without vomiting.
Anorexia is a common early symptom in appendicitis.
Fever or chills may occur from inflammatory and infectious activity.
Measured temperature can be normal, low grade, or frankly febrile depending on host and disease severity.
Pain, fever, dehydration, and inflammation can cause tachycardia.
Leukocytosis is common but not universal, especially in frail or immunomodulated hosts.
Neutrophilia is a typical blood response to acute bacterial appendiceal inflammation.
Relative neutrophilia commonly accompanies appendicitis.
CRP rises with local inflammation and tends to increase with delayed or complicated disease.
Gangrene, ischemia, and wall failure increase perforation hazard.
Contained perforation or delayed inflammation can become phlegmon or abscess.
Contained appendiceal perforation may create a rim-enhancing or drainable intra-abdominal abscess.
Perforation, abscess, phlegmon, or ongoing appendiceal infection increases procedural source-control need.
Successful appendectomy, drainage, or controlled nonoperative pathway increases source-control adequacy.
Diffuse contamination or advanced parietal irritation causes clinical peritonitis.
Uncontrolled appendiceal infection may progress to sepsis and septic shock.
Sepsis, shock, or severe hypoperfusion can raise lactate.
Severe sepsis or peritonitis can lower perfusion pressure.
Diffuse peritonitis, septic shock, organ dysfunction, and frailty increase near-term mortality hazard.
Adequate source control and active infection treatment reduce death risk.

axes.shape_free_text: Abdominal pain from visceral appendiceal inflammation or parietal peritoneal irritation.
Pain that begins centrally or periumbilically and later localizes to the right lower quadrant; may be absent in atypical anatomy or already localized presentations.
Focal right lower quadrant pain or pain maximal near the appendiceal region; location may vary with pregnancy, malrotation, left-sided appendix, retrocecal or pelvic anatomy.
Abdominal tenderness on examination, often focal in the right lower quadrant but potentially diffuse or atypically located.
Tenderness maximal near McBurney point in typical right-sided appendicitis.
Right lower quadrant pain or tenderness elicited by palpation of the left lower quadrant, reflecting peritoneal irritation.
Guarding, rebound tenderness, rigidity, percussion tenderness, or pain worsened by movement or cough from parietal peritoneal irritation.
Diffuse or generalized peritonitis from perforation, contamination, or severe inflammatory spread.
Nausea with or without vomiting caused by visceral inflammation, pain, ileus, or systemic illness.
Loss of appetite during acute appendiceal inflammation.
Subjective fever or feverishness; may be absent in early appendicitis or blunted host contexts.
Chills or rigors accompanying inflammatory or infectious appendicitis presentations.
Measured temperature, ranging from normal or low-grade fever in uncomplicated disease to higher fever in complicated or septic presentations.
Heart rate elevated by pain, fever, dehydration, systemic inflammation, or sepsis.
Respiratory rate may be normal, pain-limited, febrile, or elevated in sepsis or acidosis.
Systolic blood pressure, usually preserved in uncomplicated disease but may fall with sepsis, hypovolemia, or hemorrhagic complications.
Perfusion pressure; tends to remain normal unless severe sepsis, dehydration, or shock physiology develops.
Leukocyte count, commonly elevated in appendicitis but may be normal in early, elderly, cirrhotic, renal-failure, or immunosuppressed contexts.
Absolute neutrophil count, typically elevated with acute bacterial appendiceal inflammation.
Fraction of leukocytes that are neutrophils, often increased in appendicitis.
C-reactive protein rises with appendiceal inflammation and is often higher with delayed, perforated, or abscess-forming disease.
Lactate is generally normal in uncomplicated disease and rises mainly with shock, hypoperfusion, severe sepsis, or bowel ischemia contexts.
Qualitative imaging evidence of a dilated or enlarged appendix on ultrasound, CT, MRI, or operative pre-diagnostic imaging.
Measured appendiceal outer diameter, with values above the normal range supporting acute appendiceal inflammation in the right context.
Imaging evidence of appendiceal wall thickening, mural edema, or hyperenhancement.
Periappendiceal inflammatory fat stranding or surrounding inflammatory change on imaging.
Appendicolith, fecalith, or calcified obstructing material in or near the appendiceal lumen; present only in a subset but increases complicated and nonoperative-failure risk.
Small local, pelvic, or periappendiceal free fluid associated with inflammation or early contamination.
Secondary cecal or terminal-ileal inflammatory thickening adjacent to severe appendicitis.
Drainable or contained intra-abdominal abscess related to perforated or complicated appendicitis.
Reduced bowel motility, distension, or ileus from peritonitis, inflammation, postoperative state, or severe illness.
Daily hazard of gangrene or perforation from ongoing appendiceal inflammation, ischemia, appendicolith, delayed presentation, or uncontrolled disease.
Daily hazard of contained inflammatory mass, phlegmon, or periappendiceal abscess formation.
Daily hazard of progression to septic shock physiology from uncontrolled intra-abdominal infection or diffuse peritonitis.
Need for appendectomy, drainage, washout, resection, or structured nonoperative monitoring to control the appendiceal infectious focus.
Adequacy of achieved appendiceal source control after appendectomy, drainage, or successful monitored nonoperative therapy.
Probability that antimicrobial therapy covers likely appendiceal aerobic and anaerobic enteric pathogens and reaches the infected site.
Severe immediate or severe delayed beta-lactam reaction history constraining empiric or perioperative antibiotic choices.
Need to adjust antimicrobial dosing or avoid nephrotoxic exposure because of kidney dysfunction or renal replacement therapy.
Pregnancy context affecting anatomy, imaging modality, antibiotic selection, operative risk, and fetal considerations.
Probability that imaging or exam identifies a drainable intra-abdominal focus such as appendiceal abscess.

Probability that monitored antibiotic-based management is clinically feasible because there is no diffuse peritonitis, uncontrolled sepsis, high-risk appendicolith context, or urgent operative indication.
Probability that appendectomy or necessary operative source control can be performed promptly and safely enough to be a viable treatment vector.

Daily death hazard emergent from age, frailty, pregnancy physiology, cirrhosis, renal failure, immunosuppression, perforation, abscess, diffuse peritonitis, septic shock, delayed source control, and treatment complications.

axis_couplings.clinical_rationale: Classic migration precedes or accompanies focal right-lower-quadrant pain.
Focal RLQ pain and focal RLQ tenderness tend to co-vary in typical anatomy.
More intense local tenderness can progress to guarding or rebound as parietal irritation increases.
Dilation and wall thickening commonly appear together on imaging.
Mural inflammation can extend into adjacent fat, producing stranding.
Appendicolith-associated obstruction increases complicated appendicitis and nonoperative failure risk.
Perforation may be contained by omentum and bowel, creating phlegmon or abscess.
Abscess hazard may become imaging-visible drainable collection.
Drainable appendiceal abscess often requires drainage or operative source-control planning.
Adequate removal or control of the focus lowers ongoing perforation risk.
Source control reduces progression to septic shock in complicated intra-abdominal infection.
Septic shock is a major driver of mortality in complicated appendicitis.
Timely and adequate source control lowers death hazard.
Low perfusion pressure in sepsis or shock increases near-term mortality hazard.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Severe physiologic instability, access limitations, or anesthesia risk can delay operative source control.
Pregnancy changes anatomy and perioperative planning but does not remove the need to control appendiceal infection when indicated.

treatments.clinical_rationale: Definitive removal of the inflamed appendix provides source control for most operable acute appendicitis presentations without encoding a treatment label.

treatments.display_name: Open appendectomy, washout, or required ileocecal/cecal resection

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Diffuse contamination can make washout or open management more important.

treatments.clinical_rationale: More invasive source control may be needed for severe inflammation, perforation, diffuse peritonitis, uncertain anatomy, cecal involvement, or failure of minimally invasive control.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Antibiotic vector depends on active aerobic and anaerobic coverage.
Severe beta-lactam reactions may preclude ceftriaxone.
Antibiotics alone may be insufficient when an uncontrolled appendiceal focus persists.

treatments.clinical_rationale: A beta-lactam plus anaerobic coverage vector reduces enteric bacterial burden when active and paired with adequate source control as needed.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Severe beta-lactam reaction may preclude this regimen.
Renal impairment changes dosing and toxicity margin.

treatments.clinical_rationale: Broad aerobic and anaerobic intra-abdominal coverage can reshape bacterial burden in complicated or severe appendicitis contexts when active.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Coverage must be active against the relevant enteric pathogens.
Kidney dysfunction changes dosing and toxicity risk.

treatments.clinical_rationale: Carbapenem vector covers resistant or severe intra-abdominal contexts when susceptibility and stewardship context support it.

treatments.display_name: Nonoperative antibiotic management with close reassessment

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Diffuse peritonitis, unstable sepsis, uncontrolled obstruction, or poor reassessment access undermines nonoperative control.
Appendicolith raises obstruction persistence, recurrence, and complication risk during nonoperative treatment.
Nonoperative success requires active antibiotic coverage.

treatments.clinical_rationale: Selected monitored cases may improve without immediate appendectomy, but this vector is context-dependent and has recurrence or failure risk.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Drainage requires a safely accessible drainable collection.
Drainage alone may not control polymicrobial infection without active antibiotics.

treatments.clinical_rationale: Drainage vector controls a contained abscess focus when imaging shows an accessible collection.

treatments.display_name: Interval appendectomy after contained abscess or phlegmon control

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Persistent uncontrolled infection changes the timing and risk of delayed surgery.

treatments.clinical_rationale: After initial control of a contained complicated episode, delayed appendectomy may reduce recurrent obstruction or missed appendiceal pathology in selected contexts.

age_10_to_30_years.clinical_rationale: Appendicitis incidence is highest in adolescents and young adults.

axis_response_modulation.clinical_rationale: Older or frail patients can have muted fever or atypical symptoms.
Inflammatory lab response can be blunted or nonspecific.
Delayed recognition and reduced reserve increase complicated disease risk.
Frailty and comorbidity increase death risk after complicated intra-abdominal infection.
Pain localization can be difficult to elicit in young children.
Diagnostic delay and rapid progression raise perforation risk in young children.
Gravid uterus and appendiceal displacement can relocate pain and tenderness.
Pregnancy is a treatment and imaging context, not a disease-name subtype.
Diagnostic delay and anatomic changes may raise complicated disease risk.
Fecalith mechanically supports obstruction.
Obstruction increases gangrene and perforation risk.
Appendicolith reduces antibiotic-only feasibility and increases failure risk.
Longer untreated inflammation increases wall failure risk.
Delayed disease can become contained perforation, phlegmon, or abscess.
Delayed complicated disease often requires more complex source control.

risk_factors.display_name: Immunosuppression, diabetes, cirrhosis, or renal failure

axis_response_modulation.clinical_rationale: Host response may be blunted despite severe infection.
Leukocyte response can be blunted, exaggerated, or distorted by baseline disease or medications.
Delayed recognition and impaired host defense increase complications.
Poor physiologic reserve raises death risk in complicated appendicitis.
Atypical location can relocate pain away from classic RLQ patterns.
Classic McBurney tenderness may be absent with retrocecal, pelvic, subhepatic, left-sided, or duplicated anatomy.
Imaging may need careful anatomic search and may reveal variant anatomy.

risk_factors.display_name: Prior antibiotic exposure or healthcare-associated resistance context

axis_response_modulation.clinical_rationale: Resistant enteric organisms or recent antibiotics can reduce empiric coverage probability.

supportive_care.display_name: NPO, IV access, and perioperative preparation
supportive_care.clinical_rationale: Preparation supports safe anesthesia, imaging, and timely source control.
Fluids support perfusion in dehydration, sepsis, or perioperative states.
Symptom control improves comfort and physiologic stress without substituting for infection or source-control vectors.
Close reassessment reduces unobserved drift during diagnostic uncertainty or nonoperative management by detecting worsening early.
